title: Nullable Types
description: Understand nullable value types, the null-coalescing operators, and C# 8+ nullable reference types for writing safer, null-aware code.

data.text: **Nullable types** let you represent the absence of a value. For value types like `int` and `bool`, C# requires the `?` suffix. For reference types like `string`, C# 8 introduced **Nullable Reference Types (NRT)**, which warn you at compile time when null could slip through. Together, these features dramatically reduce the risk of null reference exceptions.

Tony Hoare, the computer scientist who introduced null references in 1965, later called it his "billion-dollar mistake." Null reference exceptions — where your program crashes because it tried to use a variable that points to nothing — are among the most common runtime errors in programming. C# gives you tools to make null explicit, trackable, and safe.
I call it my billion-dollar mistake. It was the invention of the null reference in 1965.

terms.definition: A value type (int, bool, DateTime) that can also hold null, written as int? or bool?.
A Boolean property on Nullable<T> that is true when the variable contains a real value.
Returns the underlying value from a Nullable<T>. Throws InvalidOperationException if the value is null.
Returns the left-hand operand if it is not null; otherwise returns the right-hand operand.
Assigns the right-hand value only if the left-hand variable is currently null.
A reference type annotated with ? to indicate it may be null. The compiler warns when nulls are assigned to non-nullable reference types.

data.text: Value types in C# — such as `int`, `double`, `bool`, and `DateTime` — are designed to always have a value. An `int` cannot be null by default; it defaults to 0. But in real data, a value might genuinely be missing. A database column for "Age" might be empty. A calculation might not apply. Nullable value types solve this.
Creating and Using Nullable Value Types

data.title: Nullable Value Types
data.content: Use the ? suffix to allow a value type to hold null. Use HasValue and Value to inspect it.

rows: Return left if not null, else right
Assign right only if left is null
Access member only if not null
Index only if array is not null

data.text: The null-coalescing operators let you provide fallback values cleanly. The `??` operator checks the left side; if it's not null, it returns it. If it is null, it evaluates and returns the right side. The `??=` operator only assigns if the left side is currently null, which is useful for lazy initialization.

data.title: Null-Coalescing and Null-Conditional Operators
data.content: Combine ??, ??=, and ?. to write concise null-safe code.

data.text: C# 8 introduced **Nullable Reference Types**, a compile-time feature that changes how the compiler treats reference types like `string`, `object`, and custom classes. Before C# 8, every reference type was implicitly nullable — the compiler gave no warning when you assigned null. With NRT enabled, you must explicitly mark nullable references with `?`, and the compiler warns about unsafe null usage.

data.caption: Flow of a nullable-aware method from input to safe output

data.text: You can enable NRT at the project level in your `.csproj` file, or at the top of a single file with the `#nullable enable` directive. Project-level enablement is recommended because it provides consistent protection across your entire codebase.

data.title: Enable in Your .csproj
data.text: Add <Nullable>enable</Nullable> inside a <PropertyGroup> in your .csproj file. This turns on NRT for every file in the project, giving you compile-time warnings for potential null bugs.

data.title: Nullable Reference Types in Action
data.content: With NRT enabled, the compiler distinguishes between non-nullable and nullable reference types.

data.text: The null-forgiving operator `!` tells the compiler to stop warning about a possible null reference. Use it sparingly — only when you have a strong guarantee that the value is not null, such as after an explicit null check or when working with dependency-injected services that the framework initializes.

data.title: Null-Forgiving Operator
data.content: Suppress NRT warnings when you have external knowledge that a value is non-null.

data.title: Nullable Reference Types: On vs Off

cards.title: NRT Disabled (Default in Older Projects)
cards.description: All reference types are implicitly nullable. The compiler never warns about null assignments or dereferences.

cards.title: NRT Enabled (Modern C#)
cards.description: Reference types are non-nullable by default. Use ? to explicitly allow null. Compiler warns about unsafe null usage.
pros: Catch null bugs at compile time

data.title: Gradual Adoption Strategy
data.text: If you're working on a large existing codebase, enable NRT in the .csproj with <Nullable>enable</Nullable> and treat warnings as suggestions first (<Nullable>annotations</Nullable> or <Nullable>warnings</Nullable>). Fix warnings incrementally rather than all at once.

data.title: Add Null Safety to a Person Class
data.description: Refactor a simple Person class to use nullable types and NRT properly.
steps: Create a Person class with string FirstName, string LastName, and int? Age properties.
Add a method GetFullName() that returns a string. Use the null-coalescing operator to handle a null LastName.
Add a method GetAgeDescription() that returns a string. If Age is null, return 'Age not provided'.
Create a Main method that creates two Person instances: one with all fields and one with a null LastName.
Call GetFullName() and GetAgeDescription() on both and print the results.
data.expectedOutcome: A Person class that handles nulls gracefully without crashing, demonstrating nullable value types, the null-coalescing operator, and NRT syntax.

items.question: What is the difference between int? and int? vs nullable reference types?
items.answer: int? (nullable value type) has existed since C# 2.0 and uses System.Nullable<int> under the hood. Nullable reference types (string?) are a C# 8+ compile-time feature that doesn't change runtime behavior — it only adds warnings.

items.question: Does enabling NRT change my code at runtime?
items.answer: No. NRT annotations are stripped at compile time. The runtime behavior of reference types is unchanged. NRT only adds compile-time warnings and affects IDE hints.

items.question: What does the ? after an array type mean?
items.answer: string[]? means the array itself may be null (not the elements inside it). string?[] means the array cannot be null, but individual elements may be. This distinction matters for null-checking.

items.question: When should I use ?? over if/else null checks?
items.answer: Use ?? for simple fallback values. Use if/else when you need different logic paths, logging, or when the fallback is expensive and should be lazy.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: int? makes value types nullable; HasValue checks for null
?? provides a fallback when a value is null
??= assigns only if the left side is currently null
?. safely accesses members on possibly-null references
NRT (C# 8+) warns at compile time about null bugs
! suppresses a null warning when you know the value is safe
data.takeaway: Nullable types turn null from a silent crash source into an explicit, trackable part of your type system. Always prefer nullable-aware code.
